question: Who really owns your loan?
answer: Often not the bank or brand you see. In Affirm's program agreements filed with the SEC (November 2020), Cross River Bank is the named lender, Affirm buys most of the loans, owns the customer information and services them, and Upstart processes applications and keeps the register of who owns the note. On the library's July 11, 2026 reading, the Affirm Card is issued by Evolve or Stride, not Cross River, and Upstart's note permits sale without borrower consent and discloses the owner only on written request.

items.title: The Cross River origination chain enters the public record
items.text: The program agreements filed as SEC exhibits set out the shape that later becomes standard. Cross River is the named lender. Affirm purchases most of the loans, becomes the owner of the associated customer information, and acts as the contractually designated servicer. Upstart processes applications under bank-controlled guidelines and maintains the register of who owns the note. The borrower deals with a brand that is neither the lender nor, ultimately, the owner.

items.title: The contract stack, as read on the sweep date
items.text: Read across the partner chains, the roles separate completely. For any given consumer loan, record separately **who marketed it, who underwrote it, who originated it, who funded it, who services it, who furnishes the credit data, who collects, and who ends up holding the paper.** Cross River originates for Affirm; Affirm buys most of the loans and becomes owner of the customer information. The reusable Affirm Card is issued by Evolve or Stride — not Cross River. Upstart's note permits sale without borrower consent and discloses the owner only on written request. The brand on the app is a poor guide to any of it.

items.title: Cross River raises $50M to build both sides of the trade
items.text: The parent raises $50 million to expand AI, crypto, embedded finance, international operations and product partnerships, supporting more than 100 technology partners. Cross River is simultaneously building the origination infrastructure *and* the capital that buys the resulting assets: up to $360 million of Parafin small-business receivables, a $100 million facility backed by Point home-equity-investment contracts, and up to $250 million of Figure crypto-backed loans. It can appear in a single transaction as bank, infrastructure provider, warehouse lender, or receivable buyer.

groups.label: The same split for a tokenized fund share (not a loan)
groups.note: Kept here because it is the fourth row of the same track: the fund's own filing says the transfer agent holds hosted investors' private keys and can correct errors.

items.title: Franklin's tokenized fund keeps its custodian
items.text: Franklin reports $1.79 trillion in AUM, with digital assets around $1.7 billion and growing. But the important document is the OnChain U.S. Government Money Fund's own filing, and it says this: *"For wallets that are hosted for an investor by the Fund's transfer agent, the private key associated with the investor's wallet will be held by the Fund's transfer agent."* The blockchain-integrated system is *"under the unilateral control of the transfer agent,"* which *"has the ability to correct errors."*

The 2020 program agreements are SEC exhibits; whether the same terms still apply to a loan made today depends on the agreement in force when it was made.
Arbitration clauses that travel with a sold debt are on the bank-arbitration page (Chase's 2024 replacement folds an assignee into the protected party).

catalog_context.title: What big banks are building, and the fine print behind it
catalog_context.answer: Big banks are growing by tying checking, cards, installment loans, payments and customer data into one relationship, and using AI to approve and personalize.
catalog_context.read_first: vault:02 - Research/Banking Website Sweep — Source Document.md

catalog_context.title: Banks are moving card debt to firms willing to hold it, not forgiving it
catalog_context.answer: Big lenders are selling or buying whole debt books and moving more struggling cardholders into low-rate fixed payment plans. Very little of this is forgiveness: a sale, a charge-off or a new servicer does not wipe out what the borrower owes.
